title: Bucking contest with Dutch Andrus, Sharky, Oklahoma and bad breaks
summary: He won a job at the Circle in a four-hour contest; tells of Sharky and Leon Prima, a Shawnee Oklahoma band, and why he never got a big break.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Yeah. Well it proves to you that, uh, you, uh, never know why, why I, I, uh, wanted, because I was something different that night. I played something different. I didn't play anything he played. He played something, I come out with something. No. Well the things that I played that, that night, the people never heard them, maybe. And that's, that's what won the contest, I think. Of course it was a big deal in them days. I think, just to pay about $4 a night. That was big money. Uh, Elysian Field, uh, and, uh, St. Claude, uh, right, right away, it's sweeping the store. Uh, uh, Sharky and, uh, Leon Prima opened that place up the first time. It was Sharky and Prima's band. Them, uh, two were team, teamed up one time years ago. They had a modified band, Sharky and, and Prima. Oh, and they went along for a long time. Cause I, I, Sharky, I know Sharky man when, he was playing out at Millenburg in a place every Sunday out there. And, uh, I, I, I was, well, I wasn't even playing, you know, I, I used to go out there to hear him play. I used to give a big dance out there every Sunday. I used to catch a whole train out there, they call, uh, the, uh, Smoke, Smokey Mary they used to call. And we used to go out there every Sunday to hear the band. There used to be picnics out there all day long. And, uh, gee, that's way back in the 20s. 1919, I guess. Right back. I don't know Sharky. And, uh, they were a long time together and after that they split up. They only went one way and Sharky went another way. But, uh, Sharky was, was another man too. He was a fine trumpet player, but he, he positively didn't get no breaks either in them days. But, uh, he finally got his break in the later years. And, uh, in fact he was, was one of them, man, a few trumpet players that got a break like that. Because they had some mighty good trumpet players around there. But, uh, didn't get nowhere. They had to wind up, uh, uh, on, uh, streets working or driving a truck or like Red Bullman wind up being a plumber. I wind up being an insurance man. And, uh, wind up doing something because we couldn't make the living playing music like the boys that's coming up these days. And, uh, uh, a chance in life. You know what I said? Because, uh, they were younger and, uh, well, a musician's life's a funny life. You know that. You either make it or you don't make it. You either get the break, or when you get the break, that's the time you gotta take it. Now, I, I remember one time I had a chance to get a break, play up around Chicago. And, uh, and, uh, I, uh, wanted to go up there and play. But, but I was scared, so I came back home. Another time there, I, uh, finally joined this, this, this, this, uh, band out, out in, uh, Oklahoma. Shawnee, Oklahoma was a boy by the name of Brooks Pruitt on the piano. Joe Harris trombone. Sidney Howard and clarinet. Uh, uh, Roger Boyd on the drums. There was a fine band playing, uh, uh, dance hall music out there. Now, there was, those, those, those boys that I mentioned were, were, were stars. Today they are. Harris is, is, is a big time. Roger Boyd is, is, is a big time. I played some, some way. He was from Miami, some way. Uh, Brooks Pruitt was a fine piano player. Played with Gene Goldkett and different bands. Of course, he's, he's dead now. He got killed. But, uh, I played with bands like that though, but I always wanted to come home. I would get home sick. I wanna come home. So that was just the bad breaks that I got in life. But, I mean, if I'd have kept going forward, and, uh, thought about the home life. You know, I had a family to support and all that. I, uh, think if, if I was single, I went up the line and stayed up around there up until a break came. And I, thank God, I made a little money myself. I made a little change. I, uh, think, because I could play Dixieland if they wanted Dixieland. So I was a born faker. I never knew any music. The only time I learned the, the background of music. And later years, when I took lessons from a, a man by the name of Professor, uh, Dixieland D Music from the heart, I say. Jazz music. That's the only music I ever liked to play. Is there any question you'd like to ask me?
